practice.scenario: You need an investor update deck covering last quarter: revenue up 40%, two enterprise customers signed, churn slightly worse, and a hiring ask.
practice.task: Choose the prompt most likely to produce a deck you can present without rebuilding it.

options.text: "Create a professional investor update presentation for our startup's Q3 results."

"8-slide investor update. Slide 1: headline, revenue up 40% QoQ. Slides 2 to 3: the two enterprise logos signed and what they unlock. Slide 4: churn rose from 3% to 4%, with the cause and the fix. Slides 5 to 6: hiring ask, two engineers, with the reasoning. Slide 7: risks. Slide 8: what we need from you. Direct tone, numbers in headlines, no filler."
"Make the best possible investor deck. Use your judgment on structure and make it visually stunning."

practice.revealLabel: See why the second prompt wins
practice.feedback: The second prompt wins because it supplies the two things Gamma cannot infer: the structure (how many slides and what goes on each) and the specifics (40%, 3% to 4%, two engineers). Given only a topic, the model fills space with generic business language, which is where the "AI deck" look comes from. Notice it also carries the uncomfortable number. A deck that hides worsening churn does not survive the first question, and telling the tool to include it is how you keep the argument honest. The vague prompts produce something that looks finished and says nothing.

body.html:
Gamma's output quality tracks the specificity of your prompt almost linearly. Give it a topic and you get filler with nice typography. Give it a structure and real numbers and you get a draft worth editing.

The pattern that works: state the number of slides, say what belongs on each, include your actual figures, and set a tone. It feels like more work than typing a sentence, and it is, but it replaces the twenty minutes you would otherwise spend rewriting generic content.

Presentations in Gamma now use a fixed 16:9 canvas with layouts built on grids. Content is arranged to fit the slide, so the old habit of letting a card grow to hold a long paragraph no longer works for decks. Plan one idea per slide and move detail into speaker notes.

There is also a document mode that produces long-form scrollable content instead of a slide-by-slide deck, which suits memos, reports, and proposals. Choosing the wrong mode is a common early mistake: if the output is meant to be read rather than presented, document mode is the better container.

The free plan comes with 400 one-time AI credits, and they do not refresh; paid plans provide a refreshing monthly allowance. Gamma does not charge a fixed amount per deck: credit use depends on the task, the model, and how long the generation is, so a 10-slide draft costs less than a long, image-heavy one. The free plan also caps a single prompt at 10 slides, against 100 on paid plans.

The practical consequence: do not use generation as a thinking tool. Work out your structure first, then generate once against a detailed prompt, then edit by hand. Regenerating repeatedly to "see what it comes up with" is how people burn their free credits in an afternoon and end up with a deck no better than their second attempt.

Gamma exports to PDF, PNG, and PowerPoint (PPTX), and you reach Google Slides by uploading the PPTX.

PowerPoint export is now a usable editing format. Gamma embeds your theme's heading and body fonts in the file, exports tables as real, editable tables, and includes speaker notes. Two things still need a check: italic text uses a slanted version of the regular font, and there is no slide master, so changes have to be made slide by slide.

Google Slides is where fonts change. It ignores fonts embedded in an uploaded PowerPoint file and substitutes its own, so text can reflow. If the deck is going to Google Slides, look through every slide after the upload, or pick theme fonts Google Slides already has. For a file nobody needs to edit, PDF is still the simplest handoff.

faq.q: How many free credits does Gamma give you?
faq.a: The free plan includes 400 one-time AI credits, and they do not refresh. How many a deck uses depends on its length, the model, and the task, so there is no fixed cost per deck. Free prompts generate up to 10 slides; paid plans allow up to 100 and include a refreshing monthly allowance.

faq.q: Do Gamma slides resize to fit their content?
faq.a: Not in presentations any more. The new Gamma uses a fixed 16:9 canvas with grid-based layouts, so content is arranged to fit the slide rather than the slide growing to fit the content. For long-form, scrollable writing such as memos and reports, use document mode instead.

faq.q: Can you export Gamma to PowerPoint?
faq.a: Yes. PPTX export embeds your theme's heading and body fonts, keeps tables editable, and includes speaker notes, though there is no slide master. To use Google Slides, upload the PPTX, but expect Google Slides to replace the embedded fonts with its own, so check each slide afterwards.

faq.q: How do I get a better deck out of Gamma?
faq.a: Prompt the structure rather than the topic. Say how many slides you want, what belongs on each, include your real numbers, and set a tone. A topic-only prompt produces generic filler, which is where the recognisable AI-deck look comes from.

faq.q: Is Gamma good for documents as well as presentations?
faq.a: Yes. Document mode produces long-form scrollable content rather than a slide deck, which suits memos, reports, and proposals better than a presentation format does.
